note: The plain-English layer: the front page's headline, the five questions everyone asks, the story in five moments, and a one-line plain summary for every page. Every factual sentence cites the vault slugs it rests on; the gate refuses an unknown slug.
headline: Two critical security holes in PHP, the software behind a large share of the web
deck: Nicknamed php2shell: send a request to a website running PHP, come away with a command line (a shell) on its server. Fixed on 21 October 2026. Governments told organisations that cannot update to take websites offline.

cards.a: Two flaws were found in PHP itself, the engine that runs WordPress, Drupal, Wikipedia's software and millions of other sites. Either lets anyone on the internet, with no password, run commands on the web server. The fix came out on 21 October 2026.

Not your phone or laptop: the flaw is on web servers. It affects organisations that run websites on PHP, and their visitors only indirectly. If you run a website, the question is whether PHP on its server has been updated and restarted.

Attackers have been trying: Cloudflare reports millions of attempts and Amazon a honeypot hit four days before disclosure. But no named organisation has confirmed a break-in, and CISA has not listed either flaw as exploited, as of the latest capture.

As a precaution. The US NSA and CISA said take systems offline if you cannot update them, and several governments and companies did, including Dutch government services such as DigiD. Offline is a decision, not evidence of a hack.

Update PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 (or the fixed package from your Linux distribution) and restart it. If that cannot happen today, apply the temporary settings, put a firewall in front, and as a last resort take the system offline.

moments.what: An audit spots the out-of-memory weakness. Nobody can show it is exploitable, so it is left.
Three teams using AI turn it into working attacks within three weeks and report them to PHP.
The secret leaks: the CVE numbers circulate two days early, with a wrong severity score.
PHP releases the fix a day ahead of plan. Firewall vendors already have rules live.
Agencies warn: update, or take systems offline. Sites go dark as a precaution.

pages.flaws/index.html: Two bugs deep inside PHP, in how it cleans up after an error. Both can be triggered by anyone who can reach a PHP website. Both are fixed in the same four releases.
pages.code/index.html: Where exactly the bug sits in PHP's own source code, and what the fix changed. Technical; the short version is that PHP used to abandon work mid-way when memory ran out, and now it stops safely.
pages.timeline/index.html: Everything that happened, in order, from a 2024 audit to this morning, each line tied to the page that says so.
pages.discovery/index.html: Who found the flaws (three research teams, all using AI help) and what the AI actually did, as far as anyone has said.
pages.leak/index.html: The plan was to publish the fix and the details together on 22 October. The secret leaked on the 20th; this page is the hour-by-hour account.
pages.exploitation/index.html: Every sign of attackers trying to use the flaws, in order. Lots of attempts; no confirmed break-in of a named organisation yet.
pages.impact/index.html: Two lists: who took websites offline (many, as a precaution), and who was actually broken into (nobody confirmed).
pages.defence/index.html: Can these attacks be blocked or spotted? Yes at the edge and on the server, mostly; no from ordinary web logs alone.
pages.context/index.html: How php2shell compares with famous past flaws such as Heartbleed and Log4Shell, using the official record of which ones were exploited.
pages.playbook/index.html: What an organisation that runs PHP should do, step by step, merged from every agency's advice.
pages.claims/index.html: Every statement made about the story, who made it, and how far it can be trusted, with links to the evidence.
pages.numbers/index.html: The big numbers in the headlines measure different things. 70% is a share of websites, not of the Internet; 2.6 million is a count of servers.
pages.agencies/index.html: What sixteen government cyber agencies told organisations to do. All say update; they disagree on whether to take systems offline.
pages.affected/index.html: Which PHP versions, which server setups and which software products are affected.
pages.affected/software.html: The Dutch government's list of software products and whether each is affected. A reference table.
